one_liner: Julia double-double floats (Double64, about 106-bit significand) running 6-25x faster than 128-bit BigFloat/MPFR on vector and matrix kernels.
what_it_does: Provides Double64, Double32 and Double16 (pairs of Float64/Float32/Float16) and their complex versions as AbstractFloat subtypes, so generic Julia code, including LinearAlgebra routines, runs on them unchanged. It covers arithmetic, elementary and special functions, parsing and printing, and dense linear algebra and matrix functions through GenericLinearAlgebra and GenericSchur. It is an alternative to BigFloat when about 32 decimal digits are enough, not an arbitrary-precision type.
how_it_is_fast: Each value is a non-overlapping (hi, lo) pair of hardware floats, and every operation is built from error-free transformations: two_sum (Knuth) and FMA-based two_prod (s = a*b; t = fma(a, b, -s)), so an add or multiply is a handful of native Float64 instructions with no heap allocation. Values are immutable bits types stored inline in arrays, which the project's benchmark notes name as the main advantage over BigFloat (each BigFloat is a heap-allocated MPFR object). Elementary functions use argument reduction plus fused Horner polynomial kernels, with Float128 (libquadmath) fallbacks for hard ranges.
when_to_use: Julia code that needs roughly 30-32 significant digits for ill-conditioned sums, dot products, LU/QR solves or eigenproblems: README reports 6x (elementwise exp) to 25x (elementwise multiply) less time than BigFloat at 128 bits.
Arrays and 50x50-to-64x64 matrices where BigFloat's per-element allocation dominates: the 2026 benchmark report shows 64x64 matmul at 136 us vs 15.8 ms for 256-bit BigFloat.
Mixed-precision refinement: map Float64 inputs to Double64 for the numerically sensitive part, then convert back, as the README recommends.
Replacing Quadmath.jl Float128 when 106 bits suffice: README shows 2-12x less time than Float128 on the same kernels.
when_not_to_use: You need more than about 106 bits, an exponent range wider than Float64, or MPFR-style correct rounding: use BigFloat/MPFR (or Float128 for the wider exponent).
Dense linear algebra where Float64 accuracy is enough: Double64 runs pure-Julia generic algorithms, 9-32x slower than Float64 LAPACK/BLAS in the project's report (n = 32-64).
Double32: the README itself says Float64 is better for most purposes, and 64x64 matrix exp is 1017x slower than Float32 in the report.
C or C++ projects: this is a Julia package; a C++ double-double library or a quad-precision library such as TLFloat fits there.
Hot loops calling sin/cos on large arguments, or asin/acos at all: those take Float128 paths at about 600-1,100 ns per call (input-timing report).

integration.dependencies: GenericLinearAlgebra, GenericSchur, Quadmath (GNU libquadmath), SpecialFunctions, plus stdlib LinearAlgebra, Printf, Random
integration.platforms: not documented beyond Julia's own platforms; needs a working Quadmath.jl, which is a hard dependency
integration.thread_safety: not documented; values are immutable bits types (src/Double.jl, benchmark report notes), so arithmetic has no shared state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Double64 can replace BigFloat in generic Julia code, but precision is fixed at about 106 bits (setprecision does not apply), results are not correctly rounded, and some functions BigFloat has are missing (loggamma/lgamma are exported but undefined, issue #323)

gotchas: Float64 literals are converted exactly as binary doubles: Double64(0.2) is 0.2000000000000000111..., so use df64"0.2" or Double64(2)/10 for decimal constants (README).

Large-argument trig and deep-negative exp leave the fast path: sin/cos for abs(x) >= 6.28125 go from 65 ns to about 630 ns, exp(-650) from 55 ns to 1,254 ns, and infinite inputs to sin/cos throw DomainError (docs/reports/input_timing_report.md).

Versions 1.8.0-1.9.1 computed inv with only Float64-level accuracy for inputs whose low word is zero, degrading Double64 LU residuals from 1.8e-31 to 7.9e-19 (issue #291); a muladd allocation regression from v1.10 was fixed in July 2026. Use the current 1.11 line.
Open accuracy and semantics issues: cos just below pi (#164), overflow behaviour that differs from Float64 (#151), subnormals (#181), and isapprox with tolerances beyond Float64 precision (#206).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick DoubleFloats over MultiFloats.jl when you want the broader function library (elementary, special, complex, matrix functions, generic eigen/SVD) and accept that MultiFloats claims to be 2x faster; pick BigFloat/MPFR or APFP-style accelerators when you need more than 106 bits, and TLFloat or MPLAPACK's double-double backend when the code is C++.
verified_claims_summary: The README's first-party table (BenchmarkTools on unnamed hardware, Julia version unstated) shows Double64 taking 6-25x less time than BigFloat at 128-bit precision and 2-12x less than Quadmath Float128 on 1000-element vectors and 50x50 matrices; the repo's own docs/reports/benchmarks.jl run (Julia 1.12.6, CPU not stated) adds scalar multiply 2 ns vs 41 ns and 64x64 matmul 136 us vs 15.8 ms against 256-bit BigFloat. Neither comparison is precision-matched or names the CPU.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-28, version 1.11.2), MIT-licensed, and registered in Julia's General registry under JuliaMath; usable only from Julia.
